newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector wage talks still deadlocked.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector wage talks still deadlocked.

text.p: German chemical employers and union leaders continued talks on Wednesday aimed at breaking a deadlock in the sector's 1997 wage round despite earlier disagreeing on the scope of possible labour cost reductions.
Negotiators for both sides said it was likely that the talks, which will set the wages for 590,000 workers in the industry, could now carry on late into the night.

The usually comfortable labour relations in the chemical sector have this year been disturbed by a new law introduced in October that allows German employers to cut sick-pay benefits from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
Chemical employers have agreed, following worker protests in the industry, to continue paying sick pay at 100 percent. But they want cost reductions in other areas in return.
Earlier, the IG Chemie union proposed a package under which workers would retain full sick-pay benefits but see other bonuses reduced according to absenteeism levels.

Under IG Chemie's proposal, workers would keep full sick pay with firms able to claw back costs related to absenteeism by a reduction in the "thirteenth month" end of year bonus generally given to workers.

But Hans Paul Frey, business manager for the BAVC chemical employers federation, said during a break in talks that the reduction on offer -- cutting the bonus from a full month's salary to 95 percent -- was not enough.
Sources close to the talks had earlier said the chemical employers wanted individual workers with high absenteeism rates to receive lower year-end bonuses.
But IG Chemie wanted any impact on bonuses to reflect the absenteeism of a company's whole workforce rather than just individuals.
The IG Chemie proposal put forward a system of absenteeism penalties that was based on a combination of individual and company sickness levels.
The increasingly complex dispute over sick pay has meant that the overall wage rise for workers next year had not yet even been discussed, union negotiators had confirmed earlier in the evening.
